extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for leaders about when to apologize and what an effective apology should contain (admission, expression of regret, possible restitution) to repair relationships and ameliorate harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation to apologize when you wrong someone
rubrics_metrics.description: When we wrong someone we know, even unintentionally, we are generally expected to apologize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The person we hurt feels entitled to an admission of error and an expression of regret. Leaders should recognize this social expectation and consider apologizing when they have wronged someone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apology should include admission of error
rubrics_metrics.description: The person we hurt feels entitled to an admission of error
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly acknowledge the mistake or wrongdoing rather than minimizing or deflecting; admission is a core component of a credible apology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apology should include an expression of regret
rubrics_metrics.description: The person we hurt feels entitled to ... an expression of regret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear language of regret (for example, 'I'm sorry') to communicate remorse; this emotional acknowledgment helps repair the relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer restitution or remedial action when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: We, in turn, try to ameliorate the situation by saying, 'I'm sorry,' and perhaps making restitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond words, leaders should consider practical steps to make amends (restitution, corrective action) to restore trust and address consequences of the wrongdoing.
